answer: Sensitive clays show a much more dramatic form of strain softening: after reaching peak strength, <cite id="29c94b50-0">sensitive clays undergo extensive post-peak strength degradation with increasing strain and finally disintegrate into a remolded</cite> state, and under large strains they can <cite id="29c94b50-1">transform into a remolded liquid with remarkably low shear</cite> strength. By contrast, in non-sensitive or ordinary clays, the loss of strength after disturbance is much smaller because <cite id="6c11fae6-7">Sensitivity describes the effect of soil disturbance/remoulding on shear strength</cite> and <cite id="6c11fae6-7">Sensitivity of 2 to 4 is common among normally consolidated</cite> clays. Mechanically, many non-sensitive normally consolidated clays are commonly modeled as <cite id="99aee810-4">elastic plastic strain hardening models</cite> and can <cite id="99aee810-8">adequately predict strain hardening ... for normally consolidated or lightly over-consolidated clay</cite>; when ordinary clays do soften, it is more typically a limited behavior associated with <cite id="99aee810-0">strain softening, which is an important feature of overconsolidated clay</cite>, not the extreme collapse to very low remolded strength seen in sensitive clays.

Both are common <cite id="ae3d3b8c-1">alkaline catalysts ... highly effective in transesterification, achieving rapid conversion</cite>, but in practice **sodium methoxide is usually the better-performing catalyst for clean, low-FFA feedstocks**, while **sodium hydroxide is cheaper and simpler but tends to create more soap-related problems**.

**Main differences**

- **Reactivity / conversion:** <cite id="ae3d3b8c-2">sodium methoxide [is] the most active basic catalyst</cite>. Several sources also report <cite id="ae3d3b8c-0">methoxide catalysts gave higher yields than the corresponding hydroxide</cite> and <cite id="ae3d3b8c-8">conversions of biodiesel under CH3ONa catalyst were higher than those under NaOH catalyst</cite>.
- **Soap formation:** A key advantage of sodium methoxide is that <cite id="ae3d3b8c-2">by using sodium methoxide, no more water would form, and later, the soap formation would be</cite> lower. By contrast, with hydroxide catalysts, <cite id="ac2d5b2b-2">Water causes the formation of soap through a chemical reaction called saponification. When sodium or potassium hydroxide are used as catalysts</cite>, and studies report <cite id="ac2d5b2b-7">soap formation is considerably higher than that observed with sodium methoxide</cite>.
- **Sensitivity to water / FFAs:** Base-catalyzed biodiesel production in general is sensitive because <cite id="ac2d5b2b-1">Base catalysts are very sensitive to the presence of water and free fatty</cite> acids. This matters more for NaOH because it is associated with more soap formation under wet/high-FFA conditions <cite id="ac2d5b2b-2">when sodium or potassium hydroxide are used as catalysts</cite>.
- **Handling / safety:** Sodium methoxide is harder to handle. It is commonly supplied because <cite id="ac2d5b2b-1">Sodium methoxide is sold as a 30 percent solution in methanol for easier handling</cite>, and one trade source warns <cite id="ae3d3b8c-9">sodium methoxide is highly explosive</cite>. NaOH is generally easier and more familiar to store and use.
- **Cost / practicality:** NaOH is usually favored where low catalyst cost and simple procurement matter, even though purification can be harder if soap forms. Methoxide often justifies its higher cost when producers want faster conversion, lower soap, and easier downstream separation.

**Important nuance:** performance can depend on feedstock and operating conditions. Some studies found exceptions, e.g. <cite id="ae3d3b8c-5">Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) was a more effective catalyst than sodium methoxide (NaMeO)</cite> or <cite id="ae3d3b8c-7">sodium hydroxide generally resulted in the highest yield</cite>. So the “best” choice depends on oil quality, moisture/FFA level, and process design.

**Rule of thumb**
- **Use sodium methoxide** for refined, dry, low-FFA oils when maximizing conversion and minimizing soap is the priority.
- **Use sodium hydroxide** when cost and availability matter more, and you can tightly control water/FFA or tolerate more cleanup.

**Bottom line:** For most commercial biodiesel plants using good-quality feedstock, **sodium methoxide is generally preferred over sodium hydroxide because it is more active and produces less soap**, while **sodium hydroxide remains a lower-cost but less forgiving alternative**. <cite id="ae3d3b8c-0">methoxide catalysts gave higher yields than the corresponding hydroxide</cite> <cite id="ac2d5b2b-7">soap formation is considerably higher than that observed with sodium methoxide</cite>

For Sentinel-2 land-cover classification, the most reliable preprocessing workflow is usually:

1. **Start from surface reflectance (Level-2A) rather than TOA (Level-1C)**  
   <cite id="a2045ba2-1">Level-2A data is the most ideal for research activities as it allows further analysis without applying additional atmospheric corrections.</cite>  
   If you only have Level-1C, apply atmospheric correction first; <cite id="a2045ba2-6">Sen2Cor is a Level-2A processor whose main purpose is to correct Sentinel-2 Level-1C TOA products from atmospheric effects.</cite>  
   There is also evidence that this can improve classification: <cite id="1df613e5-5">one Sentinel-2 land-cover workflow reported 82.41% overall accuracy with Level-1C imagery and 84.0% with Level-2A imagery.</cite>

2. **Do aggressive cloud, cirrus, and cloud-shadow masking**  
   Cloud contamination is one of the main avoidable error sources. Sentinel-2 provides cloud-related masks/products specifically for this purpose: <cite id="a2045ba2-7">Sentinel-2 will provide data for land cover/change classification, atmospheric correction and cloud/snow separation.</cite>  
   In practice, also mask shadows and snow where relevant, because residual contaminated pixels can be learned as false classes.

3. **Use temporally consistent, cloud-free composites instead of single scenes when possible**  
   Land cover maps are generally more stable when built from multiple observations rather than one acquisition, because compositing reduces cloud noise and captures seasonal behavior. Annual map products based on Sentinel-2 commonly use this strategy: <cite id="a2045ba2-9">each annual LULC map is produced by</cite> multi-image model inference on Sentinel-2 imagery.  
   A practical best practice is to build seasonal or annual median/percentile composites, especially where vegetation phenology helps separate classes.

4. **Exploit Sentinel-2’s multi-spectral richness, but harmonize spatial resolution first**  
   <cite id="19cac7cc-0">The 13 bands for Sentinel-2 images have spatial resolutions ranging from 10 to 60 m.</cite>  
   Because the bands are not on one native grid, resample them to a common resolution before stacking features. Most land-cover workflows use either:
   - only 10 m bands for simplicity and cleaner geometry, or
   - 10 m + selected 20 m bands resampled to 10 m to add red-edge and SWIR information.  
   Keep the resampling method fixed across all scenes and training/inference data.

5. **Include red-edge and SWIR bands when classes are spectrally similar**  
   Sentinel-2 is particularly strong for land-cover mapping because of its spectral design: <cite id="a2045ba2-0">Sentinel-2 has a positive impact on land cover/use monitoring, specifically in monitoring crop, forests, urban areas, and</cite> other surfaces.  
   In practice, red-edge bands help with vegetation discrimination, while SWIR often improves separation of built-up, bare soil, burned, and moisture-related classes.

6. **Topographically normalize mountainous areas when illumination varies strongly**  
   If your scene has steep terrain, slopes and aspect can create class confusion unrelated to real cover. Topographic/shadow correction is often worthwhile in mountain regions, especially for winter or low-sun scenes.

7. **Clip low-quality edge pixels and keep only valid observations**  
   Sentinel-2 tiles often contain edge artifacts, no-data borders, and imperfect mask boundaries. Remove these before model training so the classifier does not learn non-physical patterns.

8. **Use phenology-aware date selection**  
   Season matters for accuracy. Even if you do not build a full time series, choose acquisition windows that maximize class separability—for example peak growing season for crop/forest mapping, or leaf-off vs leaf-on combinations where deciduous/evergreen separation matters.

9. **Derive physically meaningful features after cleaning the imagery**  
   After atmospheric correction and masking, compute indices such as NDVI, NDWI, NBR, built-up or bare-soil indices if they match your class scheme. These often improve separability, but only if calculated from properly corrected and masked reflectance.

10. **Align training labels carefully with image resolution and date**  
   Even excellent preprocessing will not rescue mislabeled training data. Make sure labels:
   - match the Sentinel-2 observation year/season,
   - are co-registered to the pixel grid,
   - avoid mixed pixels along boundaries,
   - are balanced across classes and landscapes.

11. **Keep preprocessing identical for training and deployment**  
   The exact same atmospheric correction level, band set, resampling rule, masks, compositing logic, and index formulas should be used in both phases. Small inconsistencies here often reduce real-world accuracy more than model choice.

## A strong default workflow
A practical “best-practice” pipeline is:

- Acquire **Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance** <cite id="a2045ba2-1">Level-2A data is the most ideal for research activities as it allows further analysis without applying additional atmospheric corrections.</cite>  
- Mask **clouds, cirrus, shadows, snow**, and invalid edges <cite id="a2045ba2-7">Sentinel-2 provides products for cloud/snow separation.</cite>  
- Resample selected bands to a **common grid** because <cite id="19cac7cc-0">Sentinel-2 bands range from 10 to 60 m spatial resolution.</cite>  
- Build **seasonal or annual cloud-free composites**  
- Add spectral indices and optionally terrain variables  
- Train on temporally matched, quality-controlled labels  
- Validate by class and by region, not only with overall accuracy

## Bottom line
The highest-impact preprocessing choices are usually:  
<cite id="a2045ba2-1,a2045ba2-6">use atmospherically corrected Level-2A surface reflectance</cite>, <cite id="a2045ba2-7">remove clouds/snow/shadows</cite>, <cite id="19cac7cc-0">harmonize multi-resolution bands</cite>, and use <cite id="a2045ba2-9">multi-date composites rather than a single scene</cite>. Those steps typically improve class separability and reduce noise more than small classifier tweaks.

Historically, fallopian tube length has been measured mainly in two broad ways:

1. **Direct anatomic measurement of excised specimens**
   - In morphologic/anatomic studies, researchers removed <cite id="caadfe71-3,6087e8f0-0">“the whole uterus … with fallopian tubes from the cadavers to get accurate measurement of the length of fallopian tubes”</cite>.
   - This is a **physical, ex vivo measurement** of the actual tube after dissection, so it gives gross anatomic length directly rather than inferring it from an image.

2. **Radiographic visualization in living patients, especially hysterosalpingography (HSG)**
   - HSG is <cite id="ca37aa6e-2,ca37aa6e-4,c96fd64c-6">a long-established radiographic/fluoroscopic method for evaluating the uterus and fallopian tubes</cite>.
   - It uses contrast and X‑ray so clinicians can see the tubal lumen and assess <cite id="ca37aa6e-0,c96fd64c-3">the inner contour/anatomy of the tubes and whether they are patent (open)</cite>.
   - In this approach, tube dimensions are estimated from the **contrast-outlined lumen**, not from the outer wall of the tube.

How they differ:

- **What is being measured**
  - Direct dissection measures the **actual gross tube** itself <cite id="caadfe71-3,6087e8f0-0">after removal from the body</cite>.
  - HSG measures the **contrast-filled internal passage/lumen** seen on X‑ray <cite id="ca37aa6e-0,c96fd64c-3">rather than the whole external tube</cite>.

- **Setting**
  - Direct measurement is **cadaveric or surgical/ex vivo** <cite id="caadfe71-3,6087e8f0-0">on removed specimens</cite>.
  - HSG is **in vivo imaging** in living patients <cite id="ca37aa6e-1,ca37aa6e-3,c96fd64c-7">using dye and fluoroscopy/X‑ray</cite>.

- **Purpose**
  - Direct anatomy studies are mainly for **morphometry/anatomic description** <cite id="6087e8f0-0">of normal structure and variation</cite>.
  - HSG is primarily a **clinical infertility test** focused on tubal patency and luminal shape, with length only indirectly appreciable <cite id="ca37aa6e-2,ca37aa6e-4,c96fd64c-3">as part of imaging the uterine cavity and tubes</cite>.

So, in short: **older anatomic studies relied on direct ruler-based measurement of dissected tubes, whereas clinical practice has long relied on HSG, which visualizes the tube’s internal channel on X‑ray rather than measuring the whole tube directly.**

Compared with traditional nasal packing, fibrin-derived materials appear to be at least comparable overall, and in some settings better for bleeding control, but the evidence is mixed and not clearly superior across all outcomes. - For fibrin sealant, a randomized study reported substantially less postoperative hemorrhage with fibrin sealant than with nasal packing: postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9–25% of patients with nasal packing versus 3.12–4.65% in the fibrin sealant groups. - However, fibrin sealant does not consistently outperform modern absorbable packs on broader healing outcomes. In one comparison with Nasopore, no significant differences were found between the fibrin-sealant-treated side and the Nasopore-packed side for postoperative bleeding, adhesion, or other postoperative measures. - A broader systematic review concluded that, overall, no single nasal packing material can be considered optimal, and that chitosan, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and starch-derived materials showed better endoscopic scores and significant potential for use in nasal packing. For SinuBand, the available evidence is more limited: - The main published signal is that SinuBand FP was well tolerated and showed evidence of efficacy, though a larger study is needed to confirm benefits. - So, compared with other packing materials, SinuBand currently looks promising but insufficiently studied, rather than clearly superior. Bottom line: fibrin sealant may reduce postoperative bleeding compared with conventional packing, but it may perform similarly to other absorbable materials like Nasopore on bleeding and healing outcomes. SinuBand appears safe and potentially effective, but there is not enough comparative evidence yet to say it is definitively better than other postoperative packing options.

For specific strain-related benefits: 1. **LR1** - This strain is studied in the context of weaning damage, where weaning stress causes intestinal inflammation and intestinal barrier disruptions in pigs, leading to diarrhea and decreased growth performance. - So LR1’s reported benefit is mainly in **counteracting weaning-associated gut inflammation/barrier injury**, which is directly relevant to alleviating weaning stress and protecting growth. 2. **Ningxiang pig-derived L. reuteri** - A host-derived strain showed that it can improve the intestinal health of weaned piglets by modulating gut barrier function, which suggests a benefit for **barrier integrity and resilience during weaning**. - This fits the review’s point that host-specificity [is a] key propert[y] for an optimal response to probiotic supplementation in pigs. 3. **Maternal/oral L. reuteri supplementation** - Another pig study found that maternal dietary supplementation and oral administration of L. reuteri conferred the piglets with growth benefits. - This indicates some strains or administration strategies may promote **better early growth and maturation**, not just gut protection. 4. **Postbiotics derived from L. reuteri** - Though not a live-strain effect, related work shows Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets. - This suggests some strain benefits may be mediated through **bioactive metabolites**, contributing to lower stress-related oxidative damage and better survival. Overall, the best-supported benefits across different pig-associated L. reuteri strains are: - modulat[ing] the gastrointestinal microbiota - prevent[ing] post-weaning diarrhea - enhanc[ing] intestinal mucosal/gut barrier function - improv[ing] antioxidant function - promoting growth benefits So, in short: **different L. reuteri strains help weaned pigs mostly by protecting the gut during the stressful weaning period, which reduces diarrhea and inflammation and can translate into better survival, feed utilization, and growth.**

For <cite id="54fa5dda-0">people with HIV, the NIH HIV opportunistic infection guidelines were updated July 9, 2024</cite>, and screening is generally more intensive:

- <cite id="e8836bbf-0,e8836bbf-1">Ages 21–29: cervical cytology is the primary screening method, starting at the time of HIV diagnosis.</cite>
- <cite id="3257279d-1">Age 30 and older: cotesting (cervical cytology plus HPV testing) is recommended.</cite>
- <cite id="234d3932-0,234d3932-1">For women with HIV older than 29 years who have normal cotesting results, screening intervals can be prolonged</cite>—in practice, HIV-specific guidance commonly uses continued surveillance rather than the routine 5-year intervals used in average-risk women.
- <cite id="ee2137ba-1">Over age 65: continue cervical cancer screening, because people with HIV remain at higher risk.</cite>

Bottom line: <cite id="46ee0756-0">women without HIV generally screen less often and may stop after 65 if adequately screened,</cite> whereas <cite id="e8836bbf-0,3257279d-1,ee2137ba-1">women with HIV begin at age 21, use cytology alone before 30, cotesting at 30+, and usually continue screening beyond 65.</cite>

Among healthcare workers, <cite id="c37b8654-0">a self-reported history of varicella infection had sensitivity 82.3%, specificity 48.6%, positive predictive value 96.3%, and negative predictive value 14.4%</cite>. This means recall of having had chickenpox is <cite id="c37b8654-0">fairly reliable for confirming seropositivity</cite> because the PPV is high, but recall is <cite id="c37b8654-0">poor for ruling out immunity when history is negative or uncertain</cite> because specificity and especially NPV are low.

Other HCW studies point the same way: <cite id="c37b8654-5">the positive predictive value of a history of chickenpox for seropositivity was 89% (511 of 574)</cite>, and <cite id="c37b8654-8">the positive and negative predictive values of a self-reported history of varicella were 80.8% and 10.6%, respectively</cite>. In addition, <cite id="c37b8654-1">only the recall history of medical professionals had a significantly higher positive predictive value</cite>.

So, overall: <cite id="c37b8654-0,c37b8654-5,c37b8654-8">healthcare workers’ recall of a positive personal varicella history is reasonably good at predicting VZV seropositivity, but a negative or absent history is very unreliable for identifying who is actually non-immune.</cite> In practice, <cite id="c37b8654-7">a varicella infection history may not be sufficient for determination of VZV immunity</cite>, so serologic testing is preferred when immunity must be established accurately.

<cite id="4cab9042-0">Surgical masks are loose-fitting, disposable devices</cite> and <cite id="4cab9042-1">do not provide a reliable level of protection from</cite> airborne hazards, so they are less effective for inhalation protection against airborne bacterial pathogens. By contrast, <cite id="7f689a90-1">an N95 respirator is a respiratory protective device designed to achieve a very close facial fit and very efficient filtration of airborne</cite> particles, and <cite id="4cab9042-6">filters out at least 95%</cite> of them when properly used. Comparative reviews likewise find that <cite id="f73bf486-0">compared with surgical masks, N95 respirators showed less filter penetration, less face-seal leakage and less total inward leakage</cite>. For airborne bacteria specifically, <cite id="7f689a90-0">aerodynamic sizes of 800 nm or greater have been reported for airborne bacteria</cite>, and <cite id="a6b1312e-0">N95 masks could protect wearers from particles 300 nm and above in size</cite>; consistent with this, <cite id="4cab9042-8">studies have shown that surgical masks will not provide adequate protection in filtering out the TB organism</cite> while <cite id="f73bf486-2">the filter materials of N95 respirators provide good protection against TB bacteria</cite>. Overall, N95 respirators are generally more effective than surgical masks for reducing exposure to airborne bacterial pathogens, especially for wearer protection.
